title: How to Check Whether a Job Offer Is Genuine in India: A Practical Checklist
excerpt: A practical, step-by-step way to verify a recruiter, employer, job posting, and offer before sharing sensitive information or paying money.
author: TheJobInfo Editorial Team
authorBio: TheJobInfo publishes practical job-search guidance. This draft is for editorial review and is not legal advice.
content:
Finding a job can be stressful, and a message that promises quick selection or a high salary may feel like a welcome breakthrough. Unfortunately, job seekers can encounter impersonated recruiters, copied job advertisements, fake interview invitations, and requests for money or personal data. A professional-looking logo or a convincing email signature is not proof that an opportunity is real. Use the checks below before you send documents, click unfamiliar links, or make a payment.

1. Locate the opportunity on an official channel

Start from the employer's website by typing its known domain into your browser or finding it through a trusted search. Look for a careers page and search for the same job title, location, and requisition number. If the role appears only in a forwarded message or a social-media post, ask the recruiter for the original careers-page link. Open the employer website independently rather than trusting a shortened URL or a link whose visible text differs from its destination. A role missing from the careers site is not automatically fake, since hiring channels vary, but it does mean you should ask for confirmation through a contact route published by the employer.

2. Verify the recruiter using contact details you find yourself

Check whether the recruiter uses an email domain that matches the employer's real website. Look carefully for extra words, swapped letters, unusual hyphens, or a free email account presented as an official corporate address. A domain can be made to look similar without belonging to the company. Search for the recruiter on the employer's official staff directory or professional profile, but remember that profile pages can also be copied or impersonated. If anything is unclear, contact the company using a phone number or email listed on its official site and ask whether the person and vacancy are genuine. Do not use contact details supplied only in the suspicious message to verify that same message.

3. Treat requests for money as a serious warning sign

Be cautious if someone asks you to pay a registration fee, interview fee, security deposit, training charge, laptop charge, background-check fee, or refundable amount to secure a job. Do not send money to a personal bank account, wallet, QR code, or payment link as a condition of being interviewed or hired. Some legitimate employers may explain costs related to optional services or later employment arrangements, but a demand for immediate payment to guarantee selection deserves independent verification. Ask for the request and its policy in writing, then confirm it through the company's official contact channel before taking any step. Never let a short deadline pressure you into a transfer.

4. Examine the interview and selection process

Real hiring processes differ by employer, role, and location, so there is no single correct number of interview rounds. Still, be wary of an offer that arrives without a meaningful conversation about your skills, or of a recruiter who claims that a payment can replace an interview. Check the names and roles of interviewers, confirm meeting details through the original company domain, and be careful with unexpected software downloads or requests to share your screen. Do not install files sent by an unknown person just to attend an interview. If an interview link asks for credentials or permissions unrelated to the meeting, stop and verify the invitation directly.

5. Read the offer letter as a document, not a promise

Check that the employer's legal or commonly used name, role, work location, reporting relationship, compensation, joining date, and conditions are internally consistent. Compare the sender's domain with the official company domain and inspect the document for mismatched names, broken formatting, vague duties, or details copied from another company. A logo and a signature image can be copied, so they should not be your only checks. Ask the recruiter to explain unclear compensation components, probation terms, work arrangements, or conditions in writing. If the letter says that employment depends on a background check or other step, confirm what information is needed and how it will be handled through a verified channel.

6. Protect identity and financial information

Share only information reasonably needed for the stage of hiring you have reached. A resume and basic contact details are commonly needed to apply, but an unsolicited recruiter should not need your banking password, one-time password, card PIN, UPI PIN, or remote access to your device. Be especially careful with identity documents and bank details. Before sharing sensitive documents, independently confirm the employer, the recipient, why the information is required, and how to submit it securely. Do not send passwords or verification codes to anyone who claims they need them to process an application, schedule an interview, or release an offer.

7. Check for urgency, secrecy, and unrealistic claims

Pressure tactics can include a demand to act within minutes, instructions not to contact the company, guaranteed selection despite no assessment, or claims that a large salary is available for very little work. These signs do not prove fraud on their own, but they are reasons to pause. Search the exact message wording and the sender's domain, and compare the listing with the employer's public information. Be careful not to treat an online complaint as conclusive evidence either; look for multiple, independent details and verify the facts with the company. A legitimate recruiter should allow reasonable time for you to read an offer and ask basic questions.

8. Keep records and report suspicious contact

Save the job link, email headers where possible, phone number, payment details, messages, and a copy of any document. Do not delete the conversation before recording the details. If you have not paid or shared sensitive information, stop responding until you have verified the opportunity. If you have already sent money or financial details, contact your bank or payment provider promptly and ask about securing the account or disputing a transaction. In India, you can report suspected cybercrime through the official National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal at cybercrime.gov.in; for urgent financial cyber fraud, the national helpline is 1930. Use the official government portal to confirm current reporting instructions.

A quick decision checklist

  • Can I find the role or confirm it through an employer channel I reached independently?
  • Does the recruiter use a verifiable identity and a company contact route?
  • Has anyone asked me to pay to apply, interview, receive an offer, or secure a position?
  • Have I checked the offer details and verified unusual requests before sharing sensitive information?
  • Am I being pressured to act secretly or immediately?

If you cannot verify an important detail, pause and ask the employer through a trusted channel. You do not need to accuse anyone to protect yourself; simply say that you are confirming the vacancy before proceeding. A careful check may take extra time, but it is preferable to sending money or sensitive information to someone whose identity has not been established. This checklist is general job-search guidance, not legal or financial advice.
